problemText: The Islamic calendar counts its first year from the hijra, the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina, where he became a political and legal leader as well as a religious one. In what year of the Common Era did that migration take place?
choices: 570 CE
622 CE
632 CE
750 CE
hints: The migration came roughly a decade before Muhammad's death in 632 CE, and it is the event Muslims treat as year one.

problemText: After Muhammad died in 632 CE, the men who governed the Muslim community were given the title caliph. What did holding that title mean?
choices: The holder was recognized as a new prophet who received further revelation
The holder was a mystical teacher with no governing authority
The holder led the community as Muhammad's political successor without claiming prophethood
The holder was a Byzantine official appointed to administer Arabia
hints: The word names a successor in government, and Muslims regard Muhammad as the last of the prophets.

problemText: In the century after 632 CE, most Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians in newly conquered provinces continued to practice their own religions in exchange for paying a tax, and many of those regions did not become majority-Muslim for two or three hundred years. What does this pattern most directly show about the expansion?
choices: Conquered populations were required to convert before the fighting stopped
The conquerors collected no revenue from the territories they took
The expansion was carried out by traveling teachers rather than by armies
Political control changed hands far more quickly than religious belief did
hints: Ask which one changed first on the map: who governed, or what ordinary people believed.

problemText: A chronicler writing in Syria in the 630s CE recorded something like this (paraphrased): 'Our province was bled by war taxes for a generation, and the emperor's field armies had already been broken in the long Persian war; when the new armies came, several of our cities opened their gates on terms.' Which explanation of the rapid expansion of Muslim rule does this passage most directly support?
choices: The conquering armies carried gunpowder weapons that their opponents lacked
Byzantine and Persian exhaustion left border provinces unable and unwilling to mount a strong defense
Conquered cities were required to convert to Islam before any terms could be offered
Arabia had been ruled by a single powerful monarchy for centuries before 632 CE
hints: Underline only what the passage actually reports: heavy taxes, a recent draining war, and cities choosing negotiated terms over a siege.

problemText: Two Muslim scholars in the year 700 CE agree completely about the Quran, the five pillars, and the direction of prayer, yet they belong to communities that had already broken with one another. What was the original point of disagreement between those communities?
choices: Whether the pilgrimage should be made to Mecca or to Medina
Whether the Quran could be recited in Persian as well as in Arabic
Who held rightful authority to lead the community after Muhammad's death - a leader chosen by its leading figures, or a member of his family line through Ali
Whether fasting during Ramadan was required of all believers
hints: The question already tells you the two scholars share the same beliefs and practices, so the split must be about something other than doctrine. Ask what else a community must settle.

problemText: Iberia came under Muslim rule in the early 700s CE through conquest. By contrast, Islam became widespread in the West African kingdoms of Mali and Songhai and in the port cities of Southeast Asia centuries later, in places no caliph's army ever reached, beginning with rulers and merchant communities. Which conclusion do these two patterns together best support?
choices: Muslim rule and Muslim belief spread by different mechanisms on different timetables, with conquest explaining territory and commerce and teaching explaining much of the later religious map
Islam spread only where armies conquered, so later reports of merchant-led conversion must be inaccurate
Conquest and conversion always occurred together within a single generation
Umayyad armies conquered West Africa and Southeast Asia at the same time that they took Iberia
hints: Compare the two cases on two axes at once: the dates involved, and who or what actually did the spreading.
Ask whether one single explanation can cover a process that moved political control and a slower process that moved belief.

problemText: In 750 CE the Abbasid dynasty took power and soon built a new capital on the Tigris River. It became one of the largest cities in the world and home to the library and translation center known as the House of Wisdom. What city was this?
choices: Cordoba
Damascus
Cairo
Baghdad
hints: Damascus had been the Umayyad capital; the Abbasids shifted the center of the caliphate eastward toward Persia and the Silk Roads.

problemText: A book written in Baghdad around 820 CE laid out general methods for solving equations rather than a collection of separate puzzles. The English word 'algebra' comes from that book's title, and the word 'algorithm' comes from a Latinized version of its author's name. Who was the author?
choices: Ibn Sina
Al-Khwarizmi
Ibn al-Haytham
Ibn Rushd
hints: Say the word 'algorithm' slowly and listen for a name inside it.

problemText: Ibn al-Haytham (about 965 to 1040 CE) argued against the older Greek view that the eye sends out rays in order to see, holding instead that light travels from objects to the eye, and he insisted that such claims be settled by controlled experiment. Which description of his work is most accurate?
choices: He translated Greek texts faithfully without changing any of their conclusions
He rejected all Greek learning as worthless and began entirely from scratch
He corrected an inherited Greek theory and pressed for testing claims by experiment
He confirmed the Greek theory of vision by observing the sky through a telescope
hints: Notice that he keeps working on a question the Greeks asked but changes both the answer and the standard of proof.

problemText: A church official in the Spanish city of Toledo wrote around 1180 CE (paraphrased): 'Here a Jewish scholar reads the Arabic aloud in the common speech of the town, and a churchman writes it down in Latin; by this means the books of medicine and of the philosophers pass into our tongue.' What process does this description best illustrate?
choices: Arabic scholarship being rendered into Latin in a frontier city, which is how much of it reached European universities
Latin works being translated into Arabic for the use of the Abbasid court
European scholars independently rediscovering Greek science without any outside contact
Mongol armies delivering the libraries of Baghdad to scholars in Spain
hints: Track the direction the languages move in the passage: which one is the source the scholars start from, and which is the destination?

problemText: Paper-making techniques reached the Islamic world from Chinese contacts during the 700s CE and gradually replaced parchment, which was far more expensive. What effect did this most directly have on scholarship in Abbasid Baghdad?
choices: It let Baghdad's scholars print their books with movable type
It made books far cheaper to produce and copy, so libraries and the translation movement could work at a much larger scale
It removed any need to translate Greek and Indian works into Arabic
It caused the Abbasid caliphs to abandon Baghdad and move to Cairo
hints: Ask what changes for scholars when the material a book is written on drops sharply in price.

problemText: A student writes: 'Arabic numerals were invented in Baghdad, and scholars in the Islamic world mainly stored Greek books safely until Europe was ready to use them.' Which statement corrects both errors in that sentence?
choices: The digits came from Greece, and the translations were made at the request of European universities
The digits came from India, but scholars in the Islamic world did in fact limit themselves to copying Greek texts without altering them
Both claims are accurate as written, since Baghdad produced no original mathematics or medicine

The digits with place value came from India and traveled west through Arabic scholarship, and scholars in the Islamic world tested, corrected, and extended the works they translated rather than merely storing them
hints: The sentence makes two separate claims. Check each one on its own before choosing.
One claim is about ORIGIN, or where the digits came from; the other is about whether translation was the end of the work or only the beginning of it.

problemText: Song China imported a fast-ripening, drought-resistant crop from Champa, in what is now Vietnam, that allowed two harvests a year on the same land and helped push China's population past 100 million by about 1100 CE. What crop was it?
choices: A fast-ripening strain of rice
Maize brought from the Americas
Winter wheat from Central Asia
The potato
hints: The crop is usually named after the place it was brought from, and it is the grain southern Chinese farming was already built around.

problemText: In the 1020s CE the Song government began issuing printed notes that people accepted as payment, after merchants in Sichuan had already circulated paper deposit receipts. What problem was this innovation responding to?
choices: A severe shortage of paper in southern China
Trade had grown so large in volume that carrying enough copper coin to settle deals had become impractical
Confucian officials had banned the use of all metal currency
Mongol rulers demanded that tribute be paid in printed form
hints: Picture paying for a boatload of tea in strings of copper coin, then ask what the merchant physically has to haul to the dock.

problemText: The oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, was produced in China in 868 CE, and Bi Sheng developed movable type there around 1040 CE. Gutenberg's press appeared in Europe around 1450 CE. What do these dates establish?
choices: Printing reached China from Europe along the overland trade routes
Printing was invented by Mongol rulers and introduced into China after 1279 CE
Chinese printers applied the technique only to coins and never to texts
Printing was practiced in China for centuries before it appeared in Europe
hints: Put the three dates on a single line in order and count the centuries between the first two and the last.

problemText: A tax official traveling in southern China around 1180 CE noted (paraphrased): 'This district plants little grain now, for the hillsides are all under tea; the households buy their rice from boats that come up the canal, and settle their accounts with printed notes as often as with coin.' Which feature of the Song economy does this note most directly document?
choices: A return to household self-sufficiency in food
The collapse of canal transport after the loss of the north in 1127 CE
Regional specialization supported by bulk water transport and an everyday money economy
Government orders forbidding the growing of tea in southern districts
hints: The district grows one thing and buys another. Ask what has to be reliably in place before farmers dare to stop growing their own food.

problemText: The Song paid silver and silk to their northern neighbors to keep the peace, lost northern China in 1127 CE, and were finally conquered in 1279 CE. Yet historians often describe Song China as the world's most advanced economy around 1200 CE. Which statement best reconciles these facts?
choices: The tribute payments and territorial losses were invented by later writers
Military and territorial setbacks measure something different from economic strength, and the Southern Song's harvests, trade, and tax revenues kept growing after the north was lost
Song wealth was created only after 1279 CE, once Mongol rule was established
The Song economy was in fact poor, and its reputation rests entirely on its government offices
hints: Two different yardsticks are in play here: one measures armies and borders, the other measures harvests, trade, and revenue.

problemText: The Song greatly expanded the civil service examination system, so government offices were won by tested mastery of the Confucian classics rather than inherited, and cheap printed books put those texts within reach of more households. During the same centuries, foot binding spread among elite families and Neo-Confucian teaching reinforced women's subordinate legal and social position. Which summary best captures who gained and who lost in Song society?
choices: Opportunity widened for men outside the old aristocracy whose families could fund years of study, while women's mobility and standing narrowed
Opportunity widened equally for women and for men, since the tests were open to every household
Opportunity narrowed for nearly everyone, because offices returned to being inherited by birth
Opportunity widened only for the hereditary nobility, since commoners were barred from sitting the tests
hints: Handle the two groups separately first, then combine your two findings into one sentence.
Distinguish the ideal of office by merit from the real cost of a decade of classical study, and then ask whether that door was open to women at all.

problemText: In 1206 a steppe chieftain named Temujin completed the unification of the rival herding tribes of the grasslands north of China and took a new title meaning 'universal ruler.' By what title is he known?
choices: Kublai Khan
Genghis Khan
Ogedei Khan
Tamerlane
hints: One of the others was his son and successor, and another was his grandson who later ruled China. You want the man who did the uniting in 1206.

problemText: Mongol armies came out of the grasslands with no tradition of building siege machinery, yet within decades they were taking heavily walled cities across northern China and Persia. How did they overcome this limitation?
choices: They recruited and employed Chinese and Persian siege engineers from the lands they had conquered
They starved walled cities out, which normally took only a few days
They used cannon and handheld firearms, which no other army of the period possessed
They avoided walled cities altogether and took only open countryside
hints: The Mongols were known for promoting and hiring useful people regardless of origin. Ask who in the conquered lands already knew how to break down a wall.

problemText: By about 1260 CE the Mongol realm had effectively divided into four states: the Yuan Dynasty in China, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Persia, and the Golden Horde in Russia. Their rulers were relatives who increasingly acted as rivals. What does this division mean for how the empire should be described after that date?
choices: Mongol rule continued as a group of related successor states rather than as one unified government
Mongol rule ended entirely and the conquests were reversed
Mongol rule continued as a single centrally governed state until about 1400 CE
The four states were taken over by dynasties unrelated to Genghis Khan's family
hints: Ask whether the phrase 'the Mongol Empire' still names one government after four relatives begin governing four regions on their own.

problemText: A merchant's account book from the 1290s records (paraphrased): 'On the eastern road I no longer hire the twenty armed men my father hired; the khan's officers take their customs duty at the relay stations, and the road is kept.' Which conclusion about Mongol rule does this entry best support?
choices: Mongol rulers had abolished all taxes on merchants using their roads
Rulers who profited by taxing trade had a reason to protect it, which lowered merchants' costs and risks
The Mongols built the first roads ever to connect China with the Mediterranean world
Long-distance trade across Eurasia had stopped almost entirely by the 1290s
hints: Compare what the father paid for with what the son pays for, then ask who now supplies that protection and what they get out of supplying it.

problemText: Between the 1200s and the mid-1300s, knowledge of gunpowder weapons and of printing moved westward out of China, and in the 1340s a devastating plague also moved westward out of Central Asia into the Middle East and Europe. What do these two movements most have in common?
choices: Both were deliberately organized by Mongol rulers as instruments of policy
Both were carried home by European armies returning from campaigns in Central Asia
Both spread only after the Mongol khanates had collapsed and the overland routes were abandoned
Both traveled along the same fast, protected overland corridor that Mongol rule had made usable
hints: A corridor does not inspect what it carries. Ask what a new technology and a disease would each need in order to cross thousands of miles quickly.

problemText: Historians record that a Mongol army sacked Baghdad in 1258 CE, wrecking its libraries and irrigation works and ending its standing as the leading center of Islamic learning. They also record that Mongol courts brought Persian astronomers and Chinese physicians together and employed skilled officials of many origins. Which approach to the Mongol record do these two findings together best support?
choices: The destruction must be exaggerated, since a government that sponsored scholars would not level a city
The exchange of learning must be exaggerated, since conquerors do not sponsor scholarship
Both findings are accurate, and an adequate account has to hold large-scale destruction and unusually wide connection together
Neither finding is reliable, because Mongol rule left no records historians can use
hints: Notice that the question never asks you to choose a winner between the two findings.
Conquest and administration are different activities carried out at different stages. Ask whether one empire can be responsible for both.
